topic: Homeowners insurance, Cupertino: what owner-occupants report paying per year (2020-2024 survey)
value: Median falls in the $1,000 to $1,499 bracket. Of 12,741 owner-occupied homes: 4,055 pay under $1,000; 3,519 pay $1,000-$1,499; 2,003 pay $1,500-$1,999; 2,480 pay $2,000-$3,999; 684 pay $4,000 or more.
quote: Homeowners Insurance Costs by Mortgage Status (Yearly) ... Cupertino city, California ... Total: 12,741
source_name: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 5-Year Estimates, Table B25141

topic: Homeowners insurance, San Francisco: what owner-occupants report paying per year (2020-2024 survey)
value: Median falls in the $1,000 to $1,499 bracket (near its top). Of 139,057 owner-occupied homes: 38,410 pay under $1,000; 31,551 pay $1,000-$1,499; 20,630 pay $1,500-$1,999; 32,647 pay $2,000-$3,999; 15,819 pay $4,000 or more.
quote: Homeowners Insurance Costs by Mortgage Status (Yearly) ... San Francisco city, California ... Total: 139,057
source_name: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 5-Year Estimates, Table B25141

topic: Official premium quotes for a specific home (California Department of Insurance comparison tool)
note: The Department publishes a 2026 Homeowners Insurance Comparison Tool with insurer-by-insurer annual premiums for hypothetical homes by ZIP code. It is an interactive form that could not be operated from this session, so no premium was read from it. The tool states that wildfire surcharges of 15% to over 300% are not reflected in its premiums.
source_name: California Department of Insurance, 2026 Homeowners Insurance Comparison Tool

topic: Insurance premium for a tenant-occupied (rental) multi-unit building in San Francisco
note: No official source publishing a local premium for rental-dwelling (landlord) policies was found. The national regulators' report (NAIC, data for 2023, published July 2026) has California averages by policy form in its Table 4, but that table lies beyond the pages that could be read in this session. The model uses the owner's own estimate.
source_name: National Association of Insurance Commissioners, Dwelling Fire and Homeowners Insurance Report: Data for 2023

topic: Solar net energy metering: how long the legacy tariff lasts
value: Customers on the NEM 2.0 tariff may stay on it for 20 years from the date they interconnected. After that the account moves to the current net billing tariff, where exported power is usually credited below the retail rate.
quote: Pursuant to D.14-03-041, customer-generators are allowed to remain on the NEM 2.0 tariff for 20 years from the date they interconnected, or they are permitted to switch to the current tariff.
source_name: California Public Utilities Commission, Net Energy Metering and Net Billing

topic: Solar: value of surplus generation at the annual true-up
value: About $0.02 to $0.03 per kWh (net surplus compensation).
quote: The NSC rate is approximately $0.02 to $0.03 per kWh
source_name: California Public Utilities Commission, Net Energy Metering and Net Billing

topic: Property A: solar interconnection date and electricity cost after the legacy period ends
note: The interconnection date was not provided, so the year the 20-year legacy period ends is unknown. A system connected before 2030 loses legacy treatment before 2050. The model carries the owner's current small credit forward and flags it as optimistic; the later bill cannot be estimated without usage data.
source_name: California Public Utilities Commission, Net Energy Metering and Net Billing

topic: San Francisco water and sewer rates: increases proposed for July 2026 and July 2027
value: Water +7.0% each year; sewer +15.0% (July 1, 2026) and +14.5% (July 1, 2027), per the utility's presentation to its Rate Fairness Board.
quote: Water: Flat 7.0% increase to all rate schedule line items ... FYE 2027 (July 1, 2026) 7.0% 15.0% ... (July 1, 2027) 7.0% 14.5%
source_name: San Francisco Public Utilities Commission, Proposed Water and Sewer Rate Adjustments, Rate Fairness Board, March 19, 2026

topic: Cost of selling a home: real estate commissions
value: Negotiable, not set by law. Federal Reserve staff describe the traditional model as each agent being paid as much as 3 percent of the home value, with most sellers offering 2.5 or 3 percent to each side, and a downward trend over two decades.
quote: the traditional model of residential real estate broker compensation, in which the buyer's and seller's agents were each paid as much as 3 percent of the home value by the seller ... the conventional wisdom is that most sellers offer 2.5 or 3 percent commissions to both their own agent and the buyer's agent
source_name: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, FEDS Notes, Commissions and Omissions: Trends in Real Estate Broker Compensation (May 12, 2025)
